title: Disorder-promoted stability
authors: Arthur N. Montanari, Pietro Zanin, Adilson E. Motter
abstract: Previous studies of network dynamics have suggested that heterogeneity among nodes inhibits stability, at odds with the ubiquity of inherently heterogeneous natural and engineered systems. Here, we show that this conclusion arises from model reductions introduced for mathematical tractability and breaks down when nodal dynamics are higher-dimensional, yielding non-Hermitian Jacobians. In such systems, including neural, power-grid, and material networks, nodal heterogeneity can instead enhance stability, even when parameters are randomly disordered. Non-Hermiticity also underlies the stabilizing effects of network heterogeneity, which can arise even in one-dimensional nodal dynamics through nonreciprocal interactions, as shown for ecological networks. Our framework reveals disorder not as a liability but as a general resource for stabilizing complex systems.
summary: This work demonstrates that contrary to prior assumptions, node heterogeneity can promote stability in complex network systems, especially when the underlying dynamics are high-dimensional. This stabilizing effect is mathematically rooted in the non-Hermiticity of the system's Jacobian matrix. The paper establishes disorder not as a flaw, but as a general resource for enhancing the robustness of complex systems.
main_problem: The paper challenges the conventional view that node heterogeneity inhibits stability in network dynamics, particularly when simplified models are used.
main_result: Nodal heterogeneity can actively enhance stability in complex systems, a mechanism fundamentally linked to the non-Hermiticity of the system's Jacobian matrix.
method: The analysis uses linearization around equilibrium points and investigates the stability via the Jacobian matrix and Lyapunov exponents, comparing 1D vs. higher-dimensional dynamics.
model_or_system: The study analyzes general network systems, including those with higher-dimensional nodal dynamics (e.g., mechanical metamaterials, power grids), modeled by coupled differential equations.
key_observables: Largest transverse Lyapunov exponent ($\Lambda_{\max}$), stability regions (Arnold tongues), and the degree of mode mixing.
important_parameters: Nodal heterogeneity parameters ($\mathbf{b}$), network structure ($\mathbf{A}$), and the dimensionality of the nodal dynamics.
main_assumptions: Previous work often used model reductions that may misrepresent the true stability impact; the analysis focuses on continuous-time systems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate that second-order models can achieve optimal stability with heterogeneous damping, and that stability enhancement is visible across various network types and disorder strengths.
paper_structure: The paper develops a theoretical framework to show that non-Hermiticity, arising from higher-dimensional dynamics, allows disorder to act as a stabilizing resource, contrasting this with results from simplified 1D models.
why_interesting: The findings provide a general principle—that disorder can be a resource—which is highly relevant for designing robust quantum or classical networks where parameter variability is expected.
